title: Why You Need To Draw A Line In The Sand With Difficult Students ith-difficult-students/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes how some students, having learned at home that enough misbehavior gets adults to give in, bring that strategy to school and pressure teachers into unspoken deals and special treatment. He warns that accommodating this behavior — walking on eggshells, offering praise or privileges to avoid tantrums — only escalates the student's sense of entitlement and control. The alternative, he argues, is a firm internal decision that no student, no matter how disruptive, will be exempted from classroom standards, a stance that students somehow intuit and respond to even without being told directly. He acknowledges teachers may still be tested when making this shift, especially with new classes, but insists that consistently holding the line changes behavior. The piece contrasts this resolve with the 'flip side' of teachers who never draw the line and remain permanently open to manipulation.
points: Some difficult students have learned that escalating misbehavior forces adults to give in, and they bring that strategy to school.
Accommodating a difficult student's outbursts with special treatment or lowered standards only escalates their sense of entitlement.
A firm, unspoken internal decision to never negotiate classroom standards is something students intuitively sense and respond to.
Teachers making this shift should expect to be tested with anger, outbursts, or defiance before behavior changes.
Teachers who never draw this line remain permanently vulnerable to manipulation and unspoken deal-making with difficult students.
quotes: For he (or she) knows from experience that if he ratchets up his misbehavior, making it more frequent or more outrageous, the teacher will begin treating him differently.
Before long, she’ll be offering praise, prizes, and special privileges (see behavior contracts) for not disrupting the class—playing into his hands.
One of the traits that separate great teachers and classroom managers from the rest is that somewhere along the line they’ve decided not to participate in this game.
When your students know that you’ll never participate in unspoken deals, bribes, or quid pro quos, then almost magically their behavior changes.
They know that a tantrum or a dramatic stomping out of the classroom early in the year will soften the teacher up and pay dividends the rest of the way.
The only way to end the wink-wink dealmaking in your classroom, and transform your most difficult students into valued, productive citizens, is to pull the trump card out of your back pocket.
